title: What a Community Mesh Is
body:
A community mesh is a neighbourhood network built and run by the people who use it, in which small devices on rooftops and in windows pass connections along from neighbour to neighbour instead of every home depending on a single distant provider. The point is local ownership: when the network is down, a neighbour can fix it, and when it grows, neighbours decide where it grows. This record is about building and running such a network as a community project; the radio protocols underneath are covered by the device-to-device mesh technology database, and directories of existing networks are covered by the public Wi-Fi resource directory, so neither is repeated here.

How to do it: Explain the idea in one sentence to a neighbour; Sketch your street and mark homes that might host a node; List what the network should do first, such as sharing one connection or linking a hall; Agree that the network belongs to its members, not to any one person; Find one existing community network story to learn from.

What to check: Explain the mesh idea to a neighbour who has never heard of it, and sketch three possible node homes on your street. If the explanation needs jargon, simplify it before recruiting anyone.

When to stop or get help: Stop and rethink if the plan depends on one person's roof, money, or expertise. A mesh with a single point of failure is a favour, not a community network.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

title: Mapping Your Neighbourhood's Needs
body:
Mapping needs means learning, before buying anything, who in the neighbourhood struggles to get online, where the gaps are, and what a mesh could actually fix: a hall without a connection, a block with slow service, or homes that cannot afford a subscription. A simple survey, a walk with a notebook, and a conversation at a community meeting produce a map that is honest about need and modest about promises. The map also protects the project from building where it is not needed while ignoring where it is, which is the most common early mistake.

How to do it: Walk the area and note halls, blocks, shops, and dead spots; Ask neighbours what they struggle with online, in plain words; Mark needs on a simple paper map; Rank needs by urgency and by homes affected; Share the map at a community meeting before spending anything.

What to check: Present the map at a meeting and have neighbours correct it. If no one corrects anything, the map was probably not shared widely enough.

When to stop or get help: Stop buying equipment until the map exists and has been shared. Hardware bought before needs are known tends to serve the buyers, not the neighbourhood.

title: Finding Your First Volunteers
body:
A community mesh runs on volunteers with different skills, not on one expert: someone who talks to neighbours, someone comfortable on a ladder, someone who keeps notes and money, and someone who answers the phone when things break. Recruiting starts with the map and the meeting, where people can choose a role that fits their life rather than being handed a job title. The healthiest early sign is a volunteer who is not technical at all, because a network that only technicians understand will only ever serve technicians.

How to do it: Name the roles needed: organiser, installer, treasurer, supporter; Ask at the community meeting, not just online; Let people choose roles that fit their time; Pair every technical volunteer with a non-technical partner; Write down who does what and share the list.

What to check: Fill all four roles with named people, including at least one non-technical volunteer. If a role is empty, the project is not ready to build.

When to stop or get help: Stop and recruit more help if one person holds two critical roles. A mesh that collapses when one volunteer is ill has not yet become a community project.

title: Choosing Rooftops and Node Sites
body:
Choosing node sites is the practical heart of a mesh: a node needs a safe place, power, weather protection, permission from whoever owns the building, and a line of sight or a short hop to the next node. Rooftops serve streets, windows serve neighbours, and halls serve gatherings, and each site needs a written agreement about access for repairs, because a node that cannot be reached for maintenance is a node that will silently die. Safety comes before coverage: no site is worth a dangerous climb or an unpermissioned installation.

How to do it: Walk candidate sites with the installer and note power, access, and sight lines; Ask the building owner in writing before installing anything; Agree repair access times and a contact person; Prefer safe, reachable sites over dramatic high ones; Record every site and agreement in one file.

What to check: Visit three candidate sites and confirm power, permission, and repair access for each. If permission is verbal only, put it in writing before installing.

When to stop or get help: Stop any installation that needs an unsafe climb, lacks owner permission, or has no repair access. A node installed badly costs more than a node never installed.

title: A First Small Pilot
body:
A pilot is a tiny mesh, perhaps three or four nodes, built to learn rather than to impress: it connects a hall, a home, and a shop, runs for a month, and teaches the team what breaks, what neighbours actually use, and what the real costs are. Pilots protect the project from its own enthusiasm, because a neighbourhood-wide build that fails disappoints everyone, while a small pilot that struggles teaches the team quietly. The pilot's success measure is not speed or coverage, but learning: a pilot that reveals three problems is a good pilot.

How to do it: Choose three or four sites from the map; Install with written permission and safe methods; Run for a month with a simple log of faults; Ask pilot users weekly what works and what does not; Write a short pilot report before planning growth.

What to check: Run the pilot for a month and produce a report naming three lessons. If the pilot ran perfectly, suspect the log, not the luck: real pilots always teach something.

When to stop or get help: Stop expanding if the pilot's faults are not yet understood or its users are unhappy. Growth multiplies problems; it does not solve them.

title: Plain-Language Agreements with Hosts
body:
A host agreement is a short, plain-language note between the mesh group and a building owner or resident who hosts a node, covering what the device is, who may access it, who pays for power, what happens if it breaks, and how either side can end the arrangement. Plain language matters because the host is a neighbour, not a lawyer, and an agreement nobody understands will not be honoured when it matters. The agreement should be short enough to read aloud in two minutes, and it should be revisited yearly or when the host changes.

How to do it: Write the agreement in plain words on one page; Cover access, power, breakage, and ending the arrangement; Read it aloud together before signing; Give the host a copy and keep one centrally; Revisit it yearly or when the host changes.

What to check: Read the agreement aloud to a new host and confirm they can explain access, power, and ending it back to you. If they cannot, rewrite it shorter.

When to stop or get help: Stop installing on any site whose host has not agreed in plain language. An unsigned node is a dispute waiting for a repair visit to trigger it.

title: Funding: Donations, Grants, and Memberships
body:
Funding a community mesh means paying for devices, spares, and the occasional professional help, without turning the network into a business that serves paying customers first. The usual mix is small and honest: member contributions, local donations, small grants from civic bodies, and occasional fundraising, each recorded openly so members can see where money goes. The funding rule that keeps a mesh a community project is that no funder buys control: donations are welcome, but governance stays with members, and the accounts stay open to any member who asks.

How to do it: List the real costs: devices, spares, tools, and occasional professional help; Choose a funding mix of contributions, donations, and small grants; Keep accounts open to every member; Never trade governance for a donation; Publish a simple yearly account.

What to check: Present a first budget and a first account to members and answer their questions plainly. If the accounts cannot be explained to a member, they are not yet open enough.

When to stop or get help: Stop accepting any funding that buys control over the network or its rules. A mesh funded into private control is no longer a community mesh.

title: Governance: Who Decides
body:
Governance is how a mesh decides: who may join, who maintains it, how money is spent, and how disagreements are settled, written down before the first serious disagreement arrives. The lightest governance that works is usually best: a small elected steward group, open meetings, decisions recorded in plain minutes, and an annual gathering where any member can stand, question, and vote. Governance documents should be short, because a constitution nobody reads governs nobody, and they should be revisited as the mesh grows, since a four-node pilot and a forty-node network need different rules.

How to do it: Write a short governance note: membership, stewards, meetings, money, disputes; Elect stewards openly at a member meeting; Record decisions in plain minutes shared with members; Hold an annual gathering open to all members; Revisit the note as the mesh grows.

What to check: Hold a first open meeting, elect stewards, and publish plain minutes. If decisions are made in private chats instead, governance exists on paper only.

When to stop or get help: Stop and call an open meeting if stewards start deciding alone or members cannot see the minutes. Quiet governance becomes private ownership by drift.

title: Maintenance Rota and Spare Parts
body:
Maintenance is where most volunteer networks quietly fail: nodes weather, cables loosen, and a volunteer moves away, and without a rota and spares, each small failure becomes a permanent dead spot. A rota names who checks which nodes and when, a spares box holds the common replacements, and a simple fault log turns complaints into a queue that anyone can work through. The rota should be humane, with no one on call alone, and it should be celebrated, because maintenance is the unglamorous work that keeps the network alive.

How to do it: Name a checker for each node and a monthly check rhythm; Keep a spares box with common replacements; Keep a simple fault log anyone can read and add to; Pair checkers so no one works alone on roofs or ladders; Thank maintainers publicly at meetings.

What to check: Show a rota covering every node, a spares box, and a fault log with a resolved fault. If any node has no checker, the rota is incomplete.

When to stop or get help: Stop adding nodes while existing nodes sit unchecked or faulty. A mesh grows by keeping what it has alive, not by decorating the map with dead nodes.

title: Helping Neighbours Onboard and Get Support
body:
Onboarding is how a neighbour becomes a mesh member without needing technical skill: a welcome visit, a plain explanation of what the network does and does not do, help connecting a first device, and a clear way to ask for help later. Support should be human and local: a phone number, a weekly help hour at the hall, and a neighbour who can visit, rather than a ticket system that assumes digital fluency. The onboarding test is simple: a neighbour who joined last month should be able to explain the network to the next neighbour.

How to do it: Offer a welcome visit to every new member; Explain the network plainly and set up one device together; Give a phone number and a weekly help hour; Keep a one-page member guide in large print; Ask new members after a month what confused them.

What to check: Onboard a new member who then explains the network to another neighbour unaided. If new members stay dependent on one expert, onboarding has not yet worked.

When to stop or get help: Stop onboarding new members while existing members wait weeks for help. A queue of unhelped members is a warning that support, not recruitment, is the bottleneck.

title: Handling Disputes and Misuse Fairly
body:
Disputes and misuse will reach any shared network: a member who hogs the shared connection, a host who wants a node removed, or neighbours who disagree about a new site. Fair handling means written expectations agreed at joining, a calm first step of conversation, a named mediator for harder cases, and proportionate responses that start with warnings rather than disconnection. The goal is keeping neighbours as neighbours, because a network that expels members casually will soon have no community left to serve, and a network that ignores misuse will lose its hosts.

How to do it: Agree member expectations in plain words at joining; Start disputes with conversation, not sanctions; Name a mediator for harder cases; Respond in proportion, warnings before disconnection; Record outcomes plainly and keep them private to those involved.

What to check: Resolve a practice disagreement by conversation and record the outcome. If the first response to a problem is disconnection, the process is punishment, not governance.

When to stop or get help: Stop and bring in the mediator if a dispute involves threats, harassment, or illegal activity. Community process handles disagreements; it does not replace safety or law.

title: Growing from Pilot to Neighbourhood Coverage
body:
Growing from pilot to neighbourhood coverage is a staged decision, not a single leap: each new street or block is added only when the existing network is maintained, supported, and governed well enough to carry more. Growth planning revisits the needs map, recruits volunteers street by street, secures sites and permissions in advance, and keeps a reserve of spares and funds for the larger network's failures. The growth measure that matters is not node count but served people: a network that covers streets while its early members wait for help has grown in the wrong direction.

How to do it: Revisit the needs map before each growth stage; Recruit volunteers and secure sites street by street; Keep a spares and funds reserve for the larger network; Grow only when maintenance and support keep pace; Report growth to members with honest numbers.

What to check: Add one new street while keeping every existing node maintained and every member supported. If growth strains maintenance, pause growth, not maintenance.

When to stop or get help: Stop growing if maintenance, support, or governance falls behind. A mesh that cannot keep what it has has no business promising more.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

ready = ['pilot street', 'second street']

print('stages ready:', len(ready))
print('next stage:', [s for s in stages if s not in ready])

title: Working with Local Authorities and Landowners
body:
Working with local authorities and landowners turns a tolerated project into a durable one: councils, housing associations, and landlords control rooftops, halls, and permissions that a mesh needs, and they respond best to a group that arrives with a map, a pilot report, accounts, and a named contact, rather than with enthusiasm alone. The relationship should be written where it matters, such as site permissions and hall access, and maintained with regular plain reports, because officials change and memories fade. A mesh that documents its permissions survives its founders' friendships.

How to do it: Prepare a short pack: map, pilot report, accounts, governance note; Name one contact person for officials and landowners; Put site permissions and hall access in writing; Send plain progress reports regularly; Thank partners publicly and keep the relationship warm.

What to check: Secure one written permission from an authority or landowner and send a first plain report. If all permissions are verbal, the network rests on memory.

When to stop or get help: Stop installing on authority or landlord property without written permission, however friendly the conversation was. Friendliness is not permission, and permission is what survives staff changes.

title: Resilience: Outages, Storms, and Backup Power
body:
Resilience is how a mesh survives the bad week: a storm that takes down nodes, a power cut that silences a street, or a key volunteer falling ill. Resilient planning keeps spare nodes and power options ready, maps which nodes matter most, agrees what the network does during an outage, and tells members honestly what the mesh can and cannot do in an emergency. A mesh should never be presented as an emergency service unless it is tested as one; honest limits, plus neighbours checking on neighbours, beat heroic claims that fail when needed.

How to do it: Map the nodes that matter most and their power sources; Keep spare nodes and backup power ready; Agree an outage plan: what stays up, who is told, how; Tell members plainly what the mesh cannot do in an emergency; Drill the outage plan yearly.

What to check: Run a yearly outage drill and confirm the most important nodes stay up or recover. If the drill fails, revise the plan and tell members, rather than hoping for a kind storm.

When to stop or get help: Stop claiming emergency coverage the mesh has not drilled. An untested emergency claim endangers the people who believe it.

title: Measuring Whether the Mesh Serves People
body:
Measuring service means asking the people served, not admiring the map: short member surveys, uptime logs, help-queue times, and the simple count of homes that use the network weekly tell whether the mesh matters. Numbers should be honest and small: a survey that members actually answer beats a dashboard nobody reads, and a falling usage count is information, not embarrassment, because it points to the street or service that needs attention. Measurement closes the loop the needs map opened, proving whether the project kept its first promise.

How to do it: Run a short member survey twice a year; Keep simple uptime logs per node; Track help-queue times and resolution; Count homes using the network weekly; Share results plainly at member meetings and act on the worst result.

What to check: Run a first survey and share its results, including the worst finding, at a meeting. If only good news is shared, measurement is publicity, not learning.

When to stop or get help: Stop reporting node counts as success while usage or satisfaction falls. A map full of nodes that nobody uses is a monument, not a network.

title: Long-Term Sustainability and Handover
body:
Sustainability and handover decide whether a mesh outlives its founders: documented sites, permissions, accounts, passwords held properly, and routines, so that a new steward group can take over without archaeology, and a planned handover that trains successors before founders step back. The hardest part is emotional, because founders must let go of control while the network still needs them, which is why handover should be scheduled, not improvised at a crisis. A mesh with a handover plan is a community asset; a mesh without one is a personal project with members.

How to do it: Document sites, permissions, accounts, and routines in one handover file; Train successor stewards before founders step back; Schedule handover, not just hope for it; Hold credentials properly with a documented, secure method; Review the handover file yearly.

What to check: Hand a new steward the file and confirm they can run a meeting, fix a fault queue, and read the accounts from it alone. If they cannot, the file is incomplete.

When to stop or get help: Stop founders from holding sole control of credentials, money, or permissions. Sole control is the single greatest risk to a community network's future.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.
